newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania awaits Italian force as violence continues.
newsitem.headline: Albania awaits Italian force as violence continues.

text.p: The vanguard of a multinational military force was heading to Albania on Friday as fresh violence erupted in the anarchic Balkan state after several days of relative calm.

A 20-strong advance unit of Italian troops, spearheading a 6,000-strong force charged with protecting aid convoys to the stricken state, left the southeast Italian port of Brindisi on Thursday heading across the Adriatic to the Albanian port of Durres.

The continuing violence in Albania, brought to the brink of disintegration by an armed insurrection sparked by anger over failed savings schemes, was underlined on Thursday as two security officers were killed in opposite ends of the country.

The dispatch of the troops was warmly welcomed by Albanian leaders, whose original call for a large-scale international intervention force to restore order was rejected by the West, but drew a low-key response from the local press.
State-run Albanian television focused on domestic conditions and statements on domestic issues from political leaders, while barely mentioning the multinational force.
Italian officials in Albania said the soldiers were being given a specially prepared guide to the violence-ridden country that includes handy Albanian phrases such as "Drop the gun!"
In an upsurge of violence, one police officer was killed in the northern town of Skhoder late on Thursday when an armed gang drove to the police station and opened fire from their cars.
The gun battle in Albania's third largest city lasted for about 10 minutes before the assailants drove away.
In the southern town of Permet, one security guard was killed and two others injured by a group of gangsters who shot their way into a storage depot they were guarding.
The southern city of Vlore and its 80,000 residents were without water after unknown gunmen shot to pieces the electrical system of the main water pumping station during the night.
A strictly enforced 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. curfew has restored a semblance of order to the capital and surrounding area, but many regions are still considered to be lawless.
In Tirana, witnesses said about 10 heavily armed and masked officers swooped down on two men believed to be part of a group that has been firing Kalashnikov rifles into the air at night.
The police began the dawn raid by firing into the air in a show of force before grabbing the young men and beating them in full view of nearby residents. The two were taken away in vans.

More than 200 people have been killed and about 700 injured since the uprising began earlier this year when get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes failed and armed rebels took control of the south during an unchecked spasm of looting and banditry.
Army arsenals were looted after soldiers and police abandoned their posts while automatic rifles and weapons were seized by citizens who brandished them on the streets.
